messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rukmini had always been proud of her service as a midwife in the military. She had delivered countless babies in chaotic field hospitals and makeshift clinics, earning the respect of her colleagues and the gratitude of new mothers. But it was during her final deployment that something shifted inside her. A particularly harrowing night, when their unit came under attack and she found herself trapped behind enemy lines with a group of frightened civilians, left an indelible mark on her psyche. Even years after leaving the military, Rukmini couldn't shake off the feeling of being watched. She would catch glimpses of men in uniform out of the corner of her eye, or sense a male presence lurking just beyond her line of sight. These moments would send her heart racing and her mind spinning into worst-case scenarios. Being alone with men, especially those in positions of authority, made her skin crawl. Her husband, a kind and gentle man who had supported her throughout her military career, began to notice the change in her. She would pull away when he tried to hold her, or become agitated if he came up behind her unexpectedly. As time went on, Rukmini's hypervigilance only intensified. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats – a sudden movement, an unfamiliar face, a loud noise – and was always on the lookout for people who might be watching her. Even in her own home, surrounded by familiar objects and loved ones, she couldn't relax. Her mind was always racing, anticipating the next danger lurking around the corner. To cope with these feelings of perpetual unease, Rukmini threw herself into her work as a midwife. She took on extra shifts, volunteered for overtime, and immersed herself in paperwork to avoid any downtime. Her colleagues began to notice that she was distant and preoccupied, but Rukmini couldn't help it – the thought of being alone with her own thoughts was unbearable. At home, she made sure never to be alone with another person, insisting that her husband or children stay by her side even when she was doing chores or watching TV. As she became more withdrawn, Rukmini's hypervigilance only grew stronger. She began to perceive threats everywhere – in the way a stranger looked at her on the street, in the sound of footsteps outside her door, in the movement of shadows on the wall. Her husband tried to reassure her that these were just harmless coincidences, but Rukmini couldn't shake off the conviction that danger was lurking just out of sight. It was this constant state of alertness that ultimately led her back into situations that triggered the very fears she was trying to escape. A chance encounter with a male doctor at the hospital would send her spiraling back into memories of that fateful night, and she would find herself once again scanning the room for potential threats. Her husband's attempts to calm her down only seemed to make things worse – his presence reminded her of all the men in uniform who had ever made her feel small or powerless. Rukmini knew she needed help when she found herself avoiding even the simplest tasks, like grocery shopping or walking in the park, because they might put her in proximity to triggers. She was exhausted from the constant vigilance, and the strain on her relationships with loved ones was beginning to take its toll. As she sat in her therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands and glancing nervously around the room, Rukmini finally admitted what she had been trying to avoid for so long: she needed help to break free from this cycle of fear and hypervigilance that had taken over her life.
